transcript:
Header: 2025-03-15 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~72 minutes | Location: Zoom | Recording: yes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Jon Park (Redwood Product), Elena Torres (Redwood Infra), Lena Morris (Argus ML Infra), Ravi Desai (Argus Head ML), Tim Wu (Argus SRE), Sofia Karlsson (Argus Research), Martin H. (Argus Procurement)

AUTO-SUMMARY: High-level technical deep dive on quantization choices for Argus Robotics' generative models. Main focus: tradeoffs between INT8, FP8, GPTQ, and AWQ formats for latency and throughput on Redwood runtime; interactions with KV cache and large-batch scenarios; accuracy regressions and mitigation strategies; private/VPC deployment constraints and guidance for benchmarking on Argus hardware. Agreed next steps: share benchmark spreadsheet, provide traces, kickoff on-prem pilot planning.

TOPICS: 1) Baseline perf on FP16/FP32 2) INT8 quantization ops & per-layer accuracy 3) GPTQ and AWQ perceptual diffs 4) KV cache hit/miss behavior with quantized weights 5) Batching vs latency SLOs 6) VPC/on-prem deployment considerations 7) Rollout plan and fallbacks

QUESTIONS (raised by Argus): 1) How to predict accuracy regressions when moving from FP16 to INT8? 2) Does KV cache get quantized or is it unaffected? 3) What's the best rollout (canary) strategy for quantization changes in production? 4) Interaction of AWQ with our 8-bit GPUs?

TRANSCRIPT:
[00:00:00] Maya: All right everyone, thanks for joining. We're gonna dig into quantization tradeoffs — INT8, FP8, GPTQ, AWQ — with a focus on runtime, KV cache, and your on-prem constraints. I'll hand over to Samir to start with his perf overview.
[00:00:30] Samir: Cool, thanks Maya. Quick note: the numbers I mention come from internal runs and public papers, but they are workload dependent, so please treat as directional. Baseline FP16 inference gives you X latency on the model you pointed at in the questionnaire — about 120ms p50 for a 1k token context on T4-ish hardware, throughput around 50 reqs/s.
[00:01:10] Lena: Sorry can I interrupt — our platform uses mixed A100s and some older 3090s, so T4 assumptions are not exact. We care more about tail latency at 99th.
[00:01:20] Samir: Totally, thanks. For 99th pctile on mixed infra you should expect 2-3x p50 depending on batch spikes.
[00:01:40] Samir: INT8 quantization usually gives 2.5-3x token throughput improvement and 30-45% latency reduction on the fast path, but you need to watch out for layer-wise outliers — first and last layers often suffer. GPTQ and AWQ are post-training quant algorithms: GPTQ tends to be more conservative and retains quality on generative tasks; AWQ is newer and better for some autoregressive patterns but sometimes needs per-head compensation.
[00:02:20] Ravi: When you say 'per-head', are you referring to attention head scaling? How brittle is AWQ across model sizes?
[00:02:35] Samir: Yeah, attention head scaling — AWQ may require head-wise scale factors, especially on LLaMA-style blocks. We saw on a 7B model AWQ with 8-bit could match FP16 in BLEU/ROUGE in many cases, but on code-gen or reasoning prompts there were occasional regressions, like missing a step in a chain.
[00:03:05] Sofia: Is that due to rounding noise or activation distribution shifts?
[00:03:12] Samir: Both. Quantization introduces small bias in weight representation and that interacts with softmax and normalization. GPTQ often builds a per-block correction term so it can reduce that drift; AWQ focuses on asymmetric weight quant which for some layers helps but for others amplifies small errors.
[00:03:45] Tim: How does this affect KV cache exactly? If my KV cache is storing past keys/values, do we quantize those too?
[00:03:58] Elena: Good question — on Redwood runtime we keep KV cache in FP16 when using quantized weights by default, because quantizing the KV cache hurts generation quality and increases comp errors for long contexts. The cache is a hot path in memory; storing it FP16 uses more mem but preserves accuracy. We can make it INT8 if you need memory savings, but expect extra regeneration errors in long recurrences.
[00:04:35] Lena: So if we switch to INT8 weights but leave KV FP16, what's the perf win?
[00:04:42] Samir: You still get most of the compute speedup — matrix multiply is faster with int8 kernels — but memory bandwidth for KV access stays FP16 so the net throughput improvement depends on whether you are compute-bound or memory-bound. On bigger batch sizes it's compute-bound so wins are larger; on low-latency single-token cases, KV memory access is more significant and you see less improvement.
[00:05:12] Ravi: Our worst-case is single-user interactive latency at 95-99 SLO, so we can't afford quality regressions. We're prioritized on minimal regressions > 99th stability.
[00:05:24] Jon: Understood. For those SLOs we recommend a conservative rollout: start with GPTQ (it tends to be higher fidelity), test on your eval prompt set, then canary AWQ in a small pool, measure both semantic eval metrics and human review for edge cases. Also we suggest keeping an FP16 fallback route for failures.
[00:05:56] Martin: Any licensing or IP issues with GPTQ/AWQ? Procurement is asking.
[00:06:05] Maya: Generally the quant algorithms are applied to open models; some model licenses restrict modifications but most Llama-like and many huggingface models are fine; we always check per-model license. We'll include a note in the SOC2/package we send.
[00:06:26] [00:06:30] Samir: A quick table I want to call out: FP16 = highest fidelity, largest mem. INT8 (naive) = fastest but can have regressions without calibration. GPTQ = good fidelity post-hoc, quant aware correction, best for conservative rollouts. AWQ = promising perf + quality but model-dependent and sometimes brittle on small heads. FP8 — mixed bag — hardware support is limited; on Ampere+ or newer you'll get numeric gains but runtime kernels maturity varies.
[00:07:05] Lena: We have on-prem A100s and some Ampere+ equivalents. FP8 support might be possible then?
[00:07:12] Elena: If you have H100/Blackwell or dedicated Ampere+ with FP8 hardware we can enable FP8 paths, but our runtime support for FP8 kernels is behind a feature flag and we recommend stability testing. FP8 can reduce memory and improve throughput, but quantization noise again is model-dependent.
[00:07:40] Ravi: Regarding KV eviction and long rolling windows — we keep 12k tokens — do quantized weights exacerbate drift across very long generations?
[00:07:55] Samir: Yes, slight drift accumulates. If KV is FP16 it's less severe; if both weights and KV are 8-bit you will see more degeneration for very long contexts. We suggest running closed-loop prompt tests (your conversation prompts) for long-horizon drift.
[00:08:20] [00:08:30] Sofia: For evals, should we use standard BLEU/ROUGE or embedding-based semantic similarity?
[00:08:37] Jon: Both. Perf numbers often don't capture semantic shift. We recommend a small set (100-500) of representative prompts plus embedding distance thresholds and a set of deterministic assert tests (e.g., math steps, constraints).
[00:08:58] Tim: In terms of runtime knobs, what's available? Can we do per-route quant policies?
[00:09:05] Elena: Yes — Redwood supports per-route policies in the console. You can route low-risk routes to INT8/AWQ variants and keep high-risk routes on FP16. Also automated fallback: if model variant returns high perplexity/low sim, the platform can reroute to FP16.
[00:09:26] Lena: Any deployment gaps for VPC/on-prem? Network egress? We're air-gapped for some robotics control workloads.
[00:09:35] Maya: For air-gapped we do an on-prem package with a private control plane; quantized runtime is included. We need to coordinate certs and KMS access; we'll send the checklist.
[00:09:50] [00:10:00] Samir: A couple of caveats: 1) Quantization during compilation sometimes needs per-op override — we surface that as a per-model config. 2) Some optimized kernels require fused attention ops; if your model uses custom attention, we may fallback to slower paths. 3) We recommend warmup runs to populate KV cache in canary.
[00:10:30] Ravi: If we see a regression after rollout, what's the typical rollback time?
[00:10:36] Jon: With Canary + automated metrics the rollback can be immediate — route traffic back to FP16 pool. It depends on capacity but we reserve a small FP16 buffer in Dedicated deployments for that.
[00:10:52] [00:11:00] Samir: On benchmarking: you should provide live traces so we can replay and test with the same arrival pattern — steady vs spiky loads matter a lot. Also include prompt length distribution. We've put together a benchmark sheet showing p50/p95/p99 tokens/sec across INT8/GPTQ/AWQ/FP16 and KV FP16 vs KV INT8.
[00:11:30] Lena: We'll share traces. Curious about toolchain: do you support quantizing via bitsandbytes, or do you require a Redwood-specific pipeline?
[00:11:40] Samir: We support bitsandbytes for naive 8-bit, plus GPTQ tools and AWQ tooling in our toolchain. For production we often run our own calibration pass to create the quantized artifact we serve (artifact includes per-layer meta). We can ingest exported .pt/.safetensors in most formats.
[00:12:10] Sofia: Can we run mixed-precision within a single model — e.g., keep first/last layers FP16 and middle INT8?
[00:12:18] Samir: Absolutely — that's a common strategy called selective quantization. It often gives most perf benefits while minimizing quality loss. Our compiler supports layer-whitelists/blacklists for quantization.
[00:12:40] [00:12:50] Tim: Any recommendation for batch sizes relative to latency SLO — we're seeing spikes where batching hurts single-user latency.
[00:12:58] Elena: Use adaptive batching — small batch windows for interactive routes and larger batch for throughput jobs. Redwood's runtime has continuous batching that tries to keep latency under a configured SLO by dynamically sizing batches. For your 99th concerns, keep max batch small on critical routes and dedicate capacity.
[00:13:20] Ravi: On SRE side — memory fragmentation with mixed kernels, is that a concern?
[00:13:27] Elena: It can be. Mixed kernels and switching between FP16/INT8 alloc strategies can fragment memory. We mitigate with memory pools and pre-warm policies. For on-prem we recommend steady-state pools to reduce churn.
[00:13:50] [00:14:00] Maya: Quick live question: does Argus have planned traffic ramp in next 8 weeks?
[00:14:05] Lena: We expect to double traffic in April for pilot, yes.
[00:14:10] Maya: Ok then we'll plan capacity accordingly.
[00:14:20] [00:14:30] Samir: I'll call out a few empirical observations from our experience: - AWQ gave us 1.8x token throughput on a 13B in many cases with minimal perceptual loss, but on some reasoning prompts we saw 5-7% drop in exact-match. - GPTQ tends to be safer for instruction-following. - FP8 reduces memory by ~25% over FP16 but runtime kernel maturity varies. - INT4/2 are possible but require heavy retraining or advanced calibration; we don't recommend for production yet.
[00:15:10] Sofia: 5-7% exact-match is concerning for our safety checks. Do you have mitigations?
[00:15:18] Samir: Mitigations: 1) selective quantization (keep safety-related layers in FP16), 2) canary test with human review, 3) fallback routing for low-sim requests, 4) augment with lightweight rerankers/filters running in FP16.
[00:15:45] Martin: Procurement: what are pricing implications for Dedicated vs Hosted if we need FP16 fallback buffer?
[00:15:54] Maya: It increases costs modestly; Dedicated reserved capacity pricing can be structured to keep a small hot pool of FP16 nodes. We'll share example pricing scenarios after we see your trace.
[00:16:15] [00:16:30] Jon: On the runtime side, two more technical notes: - Kernel selection is dynamic: compiler chooses INT8 or FP16 matmul kernels per layer based on observed activation ranges. - We keep per-request telemetry: token timings, KV misses, quantization-induced anomalies — you can set alerts on those.
[00:16:55] Ravi: Regarding alerts — can we set a semantic-similarity threshold to trigger rollback?
[00:17:01] Jon: Yes, you can tie similarity metrics to the routing controller.
[00:17:10] [00:17:25] Samir: For the on-prem pilot we propose: 1) Replay traces w/ FP16 baseline 2) Run GPTQ quantized run (keep KV FP16) 3) Run AWQ candidate (selective FP16 for end layers) 4) Measure BLEU/embedding sim and human edge-case checks 5) Canary to small subset of traffic and compare p99 latency and accuracy metrics.
[00:17:55] Lena: That plan sounds good. What's the expected time to produce quantized artifacts?
[00:18:02] Samir: End-to-end for a 13B model usually 2-4 hours for quantization plus 1-2 hours of validation depending on your eval set. For 70B models it's longer. We'll provide tooling to automate.
[00:18:25] [00:18:40] Sofia: Any risks with model licensing when we apply GPTQ?
[00:18:46] Maya: As mentioned earlier, we review each model's license. We'll flag anything with modification-restrictions. Most permissive open weights let you quantize.
[00:18:58] [00:19:10] Tim: Network: if we keep KV in FP16, memory footprint increases — do you recommend local NVMe caching?
[00:19:18] Elena: NVMe helps for cold-cache recovery but it won't help hot path memory. FP16 KV must live on GPU memory for fast token generation. NVMe can be a fallback for infrequent large-context requests, but expect latency spike.
[00:19:40] [00:20:00] Maya: We'll wrap up soon. Anything else on regulatory or compliance for on-prem quant paths?
[00:20:08] Martin: We need audit logs for model variant changes and quantization parameters — can Redwood provide tamper-evident logs?
[00:20:16] Jon: Yes, private control plane includes audit logs and model artifact versioning; we can integrate with your SIEM and KMS for signing artifacts.
[00:20:28] [00:20:30] Samir: Final practical tip: keep a small regression test harness (50-100 edge prompts) that runs automatically after quantization compile; it catches the majority of regressions quickly.
[00:20:44] Lena: Great — we'll put that together.
[00:20:50] Maya: Recap of next steps: Samir shares benchmark sheet, Argus sends traces and sample prompts, Maya sends SOC2 and private deploy checklist, schedule pilot kickoff.
[00:21:05] Ravi: Thanks everyone.
[00:21:10] Maya: Thanks — ending recording.
